title: AI art studio
content_html:
What You'll Do

In this project you become an AI art director. You'll use DALL·E, a text-to-image AI, to turn written descriptions (called prompts) into original pictures. Instead of drawing with a pencil, you'll "draw with words" — and discover how tiny changes in your wording completely change the picture. By the end you'll have your own little gallery of AI artworks, and you'll understand how an image AI turns text into visuals.

Along the way you'll spot patterns in what works and what doesn't, find the AI's strengths and funny quirks, and think about creativity, who the "artist" really is, and bias in AI art.

What You'll Need

  • An AI image tool. Any one of these works: Bing Image Creator (bing.com/images/create, free with a Microsoft account), DALL·E via ChatGPT (chat.openai.com), or Craiyon (craiyon.com, no sign-up — a good backup if the internet is slow).
  • Somewhere to save your work — a doc or slides where you paste each prompt and a screenshot of the picture it made, so you can compare them later.
  • Good to know: free tools only let you make a limited number of images before you have to wait. Write your prompt out first, then generate — don't waste your tries on rushed ideas.

Steps

  1. Open your AI art tool. It turns a written description — a prompt — into a picture.
  2. Try a simple prompt first: "A red bicycle parked under a mango tree." Look at what the AI got right and what it got wrong.
  3. Now add detail and run it again: "A red bicycle parked under a mango tree, watercolour painting style, warm afternoon light." Compare the two pictures — see how much the extra words changed?
  4. Learn the prompt formula: Subject + Setting + Style + Mood/Lighting. Keep it handy.
  5. Try this guided prompt: "A lion wearing sunglasses, sitting on a rooftop in Nairobi, cartoon style, sunny day."
  6. Now write your own prompt using the formula. Generate it and save the result.
  7. Make at least 2 variations of your prompt — change the style, the mood, or the setting — and see how the picture changes.
  8. Pick your favourite image and write one sentence: did the AI surprise you, or match what you pictured?
  9. Share your 3 best prompts with a friend or the group — read the prompt out loud first, then show the picture and see if they guessed it.

Examples to Try

  • "A giraffe reading a book in a library, digital art style" → a colourful giraffe in glasses with an open book — a good mix of subject + action + setting + style.
  • "A futuristic matatu flying over Nairobi at sunset, comic-book style" → a vibrant picture blending something familiar with a "what if" idea.
  • Same subject, four styles: "a cat drinking tea" as a realistic photo, a watercolour, pixel art, and a pencil sketch. Notice the subject stays the same but the style keyword changes everything.

Tips

  • The AI can't read your mind. A vague prompt gives a vague, strange picture — that's not a glitch, it's a hint to be clearer.
  • Weird result? (Wrong number of fingers, garbled text, mismatched objects.) Don't hide it — ask yourself "why did that happen?" That's how these tools actually work.
  • Blocked prompt? These tools have safety filters and will refuse some things (violence, real people). If yours is blocked, reword it — don't try to sneak past the filter.
  • Save your credits. Plan your prompt before you hit generate, so you don't run out on half-formed ideas.
  • If your tool is slow or blocked, switch to Craiyon — no login needed.

Think About It

  • What is a "prompt," and why do the exact words matter so much?
  • How do you think the AI "knows" what a lion, a mango tree, or a watercolour style looks like?
  • Was there a moment the AI misunderstood you today? What might have caused it?
  • Is the picture the AI made "art"? Who's the artist — you, the AI, or both?
  • Image AIs are trained on millions of pictures made by real artists. What's good about that, and what might be a problem?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Make the same subject in 3 different styles and write one sentence comparing them.
  • Medium: Make a 4-image "story" where the same character appears in each picture — keep their description consistent so they stay recognisable.
  • Hard: Design a prompt for an abstract idea (like "friendship," "hope," or "climate change") without naming it directly, then show it to others and see if they can guess the idea.
